scenes.title: Read-the-change: baseline
scenes.objective: Locate the defender relative to a passing lane.
scenes.briefing: YOU have the puck. Teammate 1 and gold F1 are both visible. Compare their positions.
cues: YOU have the puck. Teammate 1 and gold F1 are both visible. Compare their positions.
scenes.limits: Static practice scene. Any earlier action or hypothetical change is stated in words; speed and outcomes are not simulated.

questions.prompt: Is F1 between YOU and teammate 1 in this freeze?

options.text: No, F1 is away from that passing lane
Yes, F1 is on that passing lane

questions.explanation: F1 is away from the straight lane joining YOU and 1. This describes the current picture; it does not mean a pass is always better than keeping the puck.

questions.prompt: Suppose F1 moves into the lane to teammate 1. What would you check before passing?
questions.explanation: Check whether another lane is open and whether you have space to keep the puck. If the lane to 1 has closed, you can delay or choose another option. Explain which cue would guide your choice.

questions.prompt: Which two statements match the current positions?

options.text: Teammate 1 is farther toward the right-hand net than F1
YOU have the puck
F1 is on the straight passing lane to 1
F1 has the puck

questions.explanation: Teammate 1 is farther toward the right-hand net on the overhead board, and YOU have the puck. F1 is offset from the direct passing lane.

questions.prompt: Put this scan-and-decide routine in a useful order for the current freeze.

options.text: Locate F1 and the lane to teammate 1
Check another support lane or space
Choose whether to pass, carry, or keep the puck

questions.explanation: This is one suggested scan-to-decision routine: see the pressure, check support, then choose an action. Players may scan in a slightly different order when the picture changes; the routine is not the only possible temporal action.

questions.prompt: Place teammate 1 in a support position that opens a different passing angle from YOU.
questions.explanation: A support spot with separation can give the puck carrier another angle. This is a coaching suggestion to discuss, not an objectively graded single correct location.

questions.prompt: Suppose 1 moves behind F1 along the same passing line from YOU. What is a useful next step?

options.text: Check for another passing lane
Use the same straight lane to 1

questions.explanation: In that hypothetical, the receiver has moved behind the defender on the passing line. Check for a new lane or keep the puck while another option develops.

scenes.title: Read-the-change: boards lane baseline
scenes.objective: Compare positions using the stated attack direction.
scenes.briefing: Navy teammate 1 has the puck and attacks the -x net (left net on the overhead board). Compare where gold F1 is in that attack direction.
cues: Navy teammate 1 has the puck and attacks the -x net (left net on the overhead board). Compare where gold F1 is in that attack direction.
scenes.limits: Static practice scene. Any earlier action or hypothetical change is stated in words; speed and outcomes are not simulated.

questions.prompt: Is F1 ahead of or behind teammate 1 toward the defended net?

options.text: Ahead of 1 toward the net
Behind 1, away from the net

questions.explanation: Navy attacks the -x end. F1 is farther in that direction than 1, so F1 is ahead toward the net. Being ahead does not by itself mean F1 blocks the direct lane.

questions.prompt: Suppose F1 steps into the lane from 1 to the net. What is a useful next step?

options.text: Continue through the same occupied lane
Check another route or keep the puck away from F1

questions.explanation: The hypothetical has changed the route: F1 now occupies that route. Check for another direction or space to protect the puck. The best next action depends on the space that remains.

questions.prompt: Which two statements match the starting picture?

options.text: F1 is nearer the left-hand net than 1
1 has the puck
F1 has the puck
1 is nearer the left-hand net than F1

questions.explanation: On the overhead board F1 is nearer the left-hand net. Navy 1 has the puck; the stated lane-closing movement has not occurred in this starting picture.

questions.prompt: Arrange a simple reassessment after F1 steps into the route.

options.text: Notice that the original lane changed
Scan for another lane or support
Select a puck action that fits the new space

questions.explanation: The sequence is a suggested routine for this stated change. A player can adapt the timing and may protect the puck before scanning again; it is not the sole correct temporal action.

questions.prompt: Place puck-carrying Navy 1 in a position that gives a side option away from F1.
questions.explanation: The example moves the puck carrier away from F1 and away from the nearby boards. That offers room to reassess; it is not a guaranteed escape or the only useful position.

questions.prompt: If the netward lane closes, which two alternatives could 1 assess?

options.text: Carry laterally into open ice
Keep the puck away from F1 while looking again
Continue along the same occupied line

questions.explanation: A lateral route and puck protection are alternatives to assess when the direct lane closes. Which works depends on the pressure and space at that moment.

scenes.title: Tight turn off the boards
scenes.objective: Compare the passing lanes available after a described turn.
scenes.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end (right net on the overhead board). YOU have the puck after a turn away from the boards. F1 is gold and is near the lane to teammate 2. Teammate 1 is in the middle. The earlier turn is described, not animated.
cues: Navy attacks the +x end (right net on the overhead board). YOU have the puck after a turn away from the boards. F1 is gold and is near the lane to teammate 2. Teammate 1 is in the middle. The earlier turn is described, not animated.

questions.prompt: After your turn, which passing lane is farther from F1?

options.text: The lane to teammate 1 through the middle
The lane to teammate 2 near the boards
Both lanes are equally far from F1

questions.explanation: The lane to 1 runs through the middle, farther from F1 than the lane to 2 near the boards. That gives you a clearer lane to consider in this freeze. Check again before releasing the puck; this does not guarantee a completed pass.

questions.prompt: Which statements match the current spacing?

options.text: Teammate 1 is farther from the boards than teammate 2
F1 is closer to teammate 2 than to teammate 1
YOU are farther from the side boards than teammate 2
Teammate 2 is farther from the boards than teammate 1

questions.explanation: Teammate 1 is farther inside than 2, and F1 is nearer 2 than 1. YOU are also farther inside than 2. These are current distances, not proof the earlier turn created them.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested read before releasing a pass after the turn.

options.text: Locate F1 beside the board-side passing lane
Compare the lane to 1 with the lane to 2
Recheck the chosen lane before releasing the puck

questions.explanation: The suggestion connects F1 near the boards to the two lanes, then a final check before release. Scanning can repeat; it is not a rigid rule that you must pass.

questions.prompt: Move YOU farther from the nearby side boards to change the passing angle.
questions.explanation: Moving YOU farther from the boards can create another angle to discuss. The reference is an example, not a unique correct location, and the static scene cannot prove puck protection.

questions.prompt: Why might the middle option be worth checking even though the turn began near the boards?
questions.explanation: The middle lane may be farther from F1 in this freeze, but your explanation should still mention support, pressure, and a fresh scan. The static frame cannot establish a completed pass.

questions.prompt: If F1 shifts toward the middle lane, what should YOU reassess?

options.text: The current lane to 2 and the space to keep the puck
Only the lane to 1, because it was clearer before
Only the original board-side route

questions.explanation: A shift toward the middle may change the other lane and carrying space too. Recheck the available routes; a previous comparison does not settle the next decision.

scenes.title: Pivot to close the gap
scenes.objective: Connect a described pivot with tracking the current puck threat.
scenes.briefing: Gold attacks the +x end (right net on the overhead board), which Navy defends. YOU have just pivoted and are still on the net side of F1. F1 has the puck; F2 is behind F1 in the attack direction. The pivot is stated, not animated.
cues: Gold attacks the +x end (right net on the overhead board), which Navy defends. YOU have just pivoted and are still on the net side of F1. F1 has the puck; F2 is behind F1 in the attack direction. The pivot is stated, not animated.

questions.prompt: After your pivot, which threat should YOU track first here?

options.text: F2 trailing behind the puck
The space halfway between F1 and F2
F1, the puck carrier

questions.explanation: F1 has the puck and is the immediate netward threat. Match your movement to that threat while continuing to check F2. Tracking the puck carrier first does not mean ignoring a possible pass.

questions.prompt: Which two statements match the starting picture?

options.text: F1 has the puck
YOU are closer to the right-hand net than F1
F2 is closer to the right-hand net than F1
YOU have the puck

questions.explanation: F1 carries the puck and YOU are goal-side toward the right-hand net on the overhead board. F2 trails F1 in that attack direction.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested read as you defend F1 and the trailing F2.

options.text: Locate F1, the current puck carrier
Check the trailing F2 as a possible pass receiver
Recheck possession before choosing your defending route

questions.explanation: Start with the current carrier, account for trailing support, then use the current puck location to guide your route. These checks can repeat while you move; the freeze does not show a successful pivot.

questions.prompt: Move YOU slightly closer to the middle while staying goal-side of F1.
questions.explanation: The example moves YOU nearer the centre of the ice while remaining goal-side of F1. It illustrates a possible defending position, not a completed pivot or successful gap control.

questions.prompt: What would make you change your first focus from F1 to another threat?
questions.explanation: Explain a visible change such as F1 releasing the puck or F2 becoming an immediate scoring threat. The static scene cannot establish speed, gaze, or what happens next.

questions.prompt: If F1 passes to F2, which change should YOU account for first?

options.text: Track F2 with the puck while checking F1 as support
Keep F1 as the puck carrier in the read
Treat the space halfway between them as the puck location

questions.explanation: After that hypothetical pass, F2 is the puck carrier. F1 remains a possible support threat, so account for both without treating the old possession as current.
